claims.text: Systematic variation of elemental composition governs superconducting behavior in uncharacterized high-entropy alloys.
Introducing elements with high density of states at the Fermi level is the composition change responsible for governing superconducting behavior.
The starting material is a solid solution containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 atomic percent each.
The starting material lies outside Nb-Ta and titanium-rich material classes.
Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr are candidate elements for the proposed systematic composition variation.
Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr are presented as examples relevant to increasing the density of states at the Fermi level.
The proposed relationship applies in the low-temperature regime.
Introducing high-density-of-states elements increases or otherwise favorably modifies the alloy's density of states at the Fermi level.
A higher density of states at the Fermi level enhances the superconducting pairing interaction.
Enhancement of the superconducting pairing interaction increases the superconducting critical temperature.
Introducing elements with high density of states at the Fermi level will increase the superconducting critical temperature relative to the starting material.
The proposed composition modifications must retain a solid solution with at least five elements present at no less than 5 atomic percent each.
